clinicalPearls: A prototypic cause of Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, resulting from defects in the interferon-gamma receptor chains IFNGR1 or IFNGR2.
Complete (biallelic null) deficiency causes severe, early-onset disseminated mycobacterial disease with poorly formed, multibacillary granulomata.

Partial deficiency, including the dominant-negative IFNGR1 hotspot in which a small deletion leaves a surface-accumulating truncated receptor, is milder and often presents with mycobacterial osteomyelitis.
Plasma interferon-gamma is characteristically very high because the cytokine cannot be consumed through its receptor, which is a useful diagnostic clue.
Recombinant interferon-gamma is effective only when some receptor signalling remains (partial forms) and is futile in complete deficiency.
Complete deficiency often requires haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, although very high circulating interferon-gamma can compromise engraftment.
Live BCG vaccination frequently unmasks the disorder as disseminated BCG disease.
reference.pathophysiology: The interferon-gamma receptor is a heterotetramer of two ligand-binding IFNGR1 chains and two signal-transducing IFNGR2 chains; ligand engagement activates receptor-associated JAK1 and JAK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 to form the gamma-activated factor homodimer that transcribes genes arming mononuclear phagocytes against intracellular pathogens. Loss-of-function mutations in IFNGR1 or IFNGR2 abolish or attenuate this signal. Complete recessive deficiency leaves macrophages unable to respond to interferon-gamma, producing severe multibacillary disease, whereas partial recessive and partial dominant forms retain some signalling. A recurrent small-deletion hotspot in IFNGR1 generates a truncated receptor lacking the intracellular recycling and degradation motif; the receptor accumulates on the cell surface and acts in a dominant-negative fashion, the basis of autosomal dominant partial deficiency. Because interferon-gamma is normally internalised and consumed through its receptor, defective receptors lead to strikingly elevated circulating interferon-gamma.
additionalDifferentials: IL-12/IL-23 axis defects (IL12B, IL12RB1) causing MSMD
Disseminated tuberculosis or leprosy in an apparently immunocompetent host
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry for IFNGR1 and IFNGR2 surface expression, including detection of accumulated truncated receptor
Assay of STAT1 phosphorylation and downstream gene induction after interferon-gamma stimulation
Plasma interferon-gamma concentration, typically strikingly elevated
Mycobacterial culture with species identification and typing
Tissue biopsy for granuloma morphology and bacillary load
Whole-blood functional immunoassays of the IL-12-interferon-gamma circuit
redFlags: Disseminated BCG or non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease in infancy
Mycobacterial osteomyelitis, a signature of partial dominant deficiency
Relentless mycobacterial disease despite adequate antimicrobial therapy
Very high circulating interferon-gamma in the presence of ongoing mycobacterial infection
reference.prognosis: Partial forms often have a good outlook with prolonged antimycobacterial therapy and recombinant interferon-gamma, whereas complete receptor deficiency has a poor prognosis and is frequently fatal without haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which is itself complicated by high interferon-gamma levels.
pitfalls: Prescribing recombinant interferon-gamma in complete deficiency, where it cannot act.
Interpreting a high plasma interferon-gamma as reassuring rather than as a marker of receptor failure.
Missing surface-accumulated truncated receptor unless it is specifically sought on flow cytometry.
Confusing BCG disease with tuberculosis without species typing.
Delaying transplant assessment in complete deficiency.
references: International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS) inborn errors of immunity classification
management: Treat mycobacterial infections with prolonged multidrug antimycobacterial regimens, often lifelong, guided by species identification and susceptibility
Reserve recombinant interferon-gamma for partial forms with residual signalling, as it is futile in complete receptor deficiency
Offer allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for complete deficiency, recognising that very high circulating interferon-gamma can compromise engraftment
Use long-term macrolide-based antimycobacterial prophylaxis and strictly avoid live BCG and other live vaccines
Manage disseminated disease and febrile deterioration aggressively with cultures and directed antimicrobials
Monitor with serial mycobacterial cultures, inflammatory markers and imaging for relapse
Provide genetic counselling and cascade family screening for this recessively inherited disorder
